segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay, um, I think we're all here.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So welcome everyone, this is our kick-off meeting.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I'm Laura, I'll be the project manager for this one.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Um, maybe we just go round and say who we are?

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Yeah, uh, I'm Tomasz, I'm the industrial designer.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: So, um, the casing, the components, what's actually inside it.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: I'm Priya, user interface design.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: So how people actually, uh, talk to it and what it does back.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: And I'm Ben, marketing.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Uh, finding out what people want and what they'll pay for.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Great.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay so the project. We're designing a kitchen timer.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: But a voice-controlled one.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Oh okay.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So the idea is you're cooking, your hands are covered in flour or whatever, and you just say set ten minutes.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: That actually makes a lot of sense.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Yeah, I've had that, with like, raw chicken hands.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So the agenda for today, um, it's quite short.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Getting to know each other, which we've sort of done, the budget, and then just some first ideas.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And then I'll hand out what everyone's doing before the next meeting.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Okay.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So, um, the money side first.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: We're aiming to sell it for twenty-five euros.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And the production cost per unit can't go over twelve fifty.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Twelve fifty per unit?

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Per unit, yeah.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And the company wants, uh, fifteen million profit overall.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Hmm, twelve fifty with a speech chip in it. That's tight.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Does it have to recognise speech on the device itself or could it, like, use your phone?

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Um, well -

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Because if it's on the phone then the timer's basically just a speaker.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Yeah, but then you need the phone near you, and it's in your pocket with flour all over it.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Yeah, people won't want to pair it with an app just to boil an egg.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Fair.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: I'd say on-device, just a small set of commands. Like, set, stop, how long left.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Mm, a fixed vocabulary is much easier to get right.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So, on the device, limited commands.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: But that goes back to the money though, because that chip has to fit in twelve fifty.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Yeah. I mean the simple command chips aren't that expensive, I think maybe three, four euros.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: But then you've got the mic, the speaker, the case, battery...

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: And does twenty-five euros sound right for this, like, to the customer?

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Because a normal kitchen timer is what, five euros?

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Twenty-five is what management's given us, so.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Right, so it's got to feel premium then.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Maybe a little screen with recipe suggestions, wifi, that kind of thing.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Sure, and for twelve fifty we'll throw in a free fridge with every one.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Ha, yeah.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Yeah, I don't think wifi and a recipe screen fit in that budget.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Okay, okay, fair enough.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Can I go back to the voice thing for a sec?

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Yeah, go on.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: How does it know you're talking to it? Like, the radio's on, people are chatting in the kitchen.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Wake word. You say like 'timer' first.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Yeah, but 'timer' is a normal word, you'll trigger it by accident.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Give it a name? Like a little brand name.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: That could work, something you wouldn't normally say.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: And that's good for marketing as well, actually, people like naming stuff.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So some kind of wake word, probably a name.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Yeah, and um -

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: I'd still want one physical button though. For stopping the alarm.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Why, if it's voice?

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Because when it's beeping it's loud and it might not hear you over itself.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Oh, yeah, true.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Everyone okay with one button as a backup?

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay, one physical button, mainly for stopping the alarm.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Which actually helps on cost, a button's like nothing.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: The bigger cost question is power. Batteries or plugged in.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: If it's always listening for the wake word, batteries will drain fast.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: But plugged in means a cable across the worktop, which is a bit annoying.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And a mains adapter adds cost too.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So what would you lean towards?

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Uh, honestly I don't know yet.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: I'll have to look at what the components cost and what the power draw is.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay, so that's open for now.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Oh, and on the voice side, it should talk back, I think.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Like if you say ten minutes, it says 'ten minutes, started' so you know it heard.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Yeah, otherwise you're standing there wondering.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Short responses though, not a whole sentence.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: And multiple timers? Like pasta and the sauce at the same time?

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I'd love that personally.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: That's more a software thing, shouldn't change the hardware much.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: I can think about how you'd name them, like 'pasta timer'.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay, um, we're running out of time, so let's sort what everyone's doing.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Next meeting's in about thirty minutes, that's the functional design one.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Tomasz, can you look at the components, the speech chip, mic, speaker, and the power question?

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Yep, I'll do that.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And I'll try to get a rough cost breakdown against the twelve fifty.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Priya, the voice commands, so the wake word, the command list, the talking back.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Yep, and the multiple timers.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Yeah, good.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Ben, can you find out what people actually want from a kitchen timer?

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Yeah, I'll look at what's out there and what people complain about.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: I can also check if anyone actually pays twenty-five for a timer.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Yeah, that'd be useful.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Should someone look into the name for the wake word? Or is that later?

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: I can throw some names around, it's kind of marketing.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Cool.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And I'll write up the minutes and send them round.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Anything else?

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Um, no, I think that's it.

segments.speaker: D
segments.text: Nope.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Okay, thanks everyone, see you in a bit.

segments.speaker: C
segments.text: Thanks.

abstract: The project manager opened the kick-off meeting, the team members introduced themselves and their roles, and the project manager introduced the project: a voice-controlled kitchen timer that people can use when their hands are dirty from cooking.
The project manager presented the financial targets: a selling price of 25 euros, a maximum production cost of 12.50 euros per unit and an overall profit target of 15 million euros.

On the budget, the industrial designer estimated a simple command-recognition chip at three to four euros and raised the open question of battery versus mains power, since always listening for a wake word drains batteries and a mains adapter adds cost. The marketing expert's idea of a recipe screen with wifi was judged not to fit the budget.

On voice interaction, the team agreed that speech recognition should run on the device with a small fixed set of commands rather than through a phone app. It should use a wake word, probably a distinctive product name. It should give short spoken confirmations, and one physical button should serve as a backup for stopping the alarm.
Support for multiple named timers was raised as a mainly software feature to explore, and individual research tasks were assigned before the functional design meeting.
actions: The industrial designer will research the components (speech chip, microphone, speaker) and the power question, and produce a rough cost breakdown against the 12.50 euro limit.
The user interface designer will work out the voice interaction: wake word, command list, spoken feedback and multiple timers.
The marketing expert will research what users want from kitchen timers, what they complain about, and whether customers will pay 25 euros for a timer.
The marketing expert will come up with candidate names for the wake word.
The project manager will write up the minutes and send them to the team.
decisions: The target selling price is 25 euros and production cost must not exceed 12.50 euros per unit.
Speech recognition will run on the device itself with a small fixed command set (e.g. set, stop, how long left), not via a phone app.
The timer will use a wake word, probably a distinctive name rather than a common word like 'timer'.
The timer will have one physical button as a backup, mainly for stopping the alarm.
The timer will give short spoken confirmations of commands.
A recipe screen with wifi is out of scope because it does not fit the budget.
problems: Whether the timer will run on batteries or mains power is still open, because always-on listening drains batteries while a mains adapter adds cost and a cable.
It is not yet known whether all components fit within 12.50 euros.
The marketing expert questioned whether customers will pay 25 euros when ordinary kitchen timers cost around five euros.
Support for multiple simultaneous timers was raised but not yet decided.
